analysis.one_liner: Freezes nearly all new federal regulations from taking effect for almost two years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred federal agencies from issuing new rules until early 2013, was introduced in March 2011 and never advanced past its subcommittee referrals, dying without a vote when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped every federal department and agency from putting new rules into force until January 31, 2013. Rules dealing with the military, foreign affairs, agency management, and benefits like loans, grants, and contracts were carved out, but rules that protect workers, consumers, public health, and the environment would have been frozen. New safety standards, pollution limits, and financial protections — everything agencies had in the pipeline — would have waited on hold while regulated businesses kept operating under the old, weaker rules. The bill was referred to two House committees and two subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries gain most: a company facing a new pollution limit, workplace safety standard, or consumer protection rule gets to delay complying with it, saving money for the duration of the freeze. Businesses that had spent money lobbying against specific upcoming rules would get a blanket two-year delay covering all of them at once.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any federal department or agency from putting a rule into force until January 31, 2013, so any business facing an upcoming requirement gets roughly a two-year reprieve. [S2][S3]
The freeze applies across the entire government at once, rather than through case-by-case review, so rules already in the pipeline — some years in the making — would be stopped together. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections pay. Rules that would have limited air and water pollution, set workplace safety standards, protected consumers from unsafe products, or constrained risky financial practices would not take effect, and the hazards those rules were written to address would continue unaddressed during the freeze. Agencies would also have to shelve work on rules already in progress.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal protections

drawbacks.text: A blanket freeze is indiscriminate: it blocks good rules and bad rules alike, rather than reviewing each one on its merits, and it would discard agency work on rules already underway. [S2][S3]

The two-year delay shifts real risks onto the public — delayed pollution limits, workplace safety standards, and consumer protections mean the harms those rules targeted continue during the freeze. [S2]

Even supporters of lighter regulation generally pursue it through reviewing or rescinding individual rules; a blanket moratorium removes the government's ability to respond to new hazards that emerge during the freeze period. [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall heavily on the public. The bill's benefit to businesses is straightforward — fewer new requirements for two years — but the price is that every protective rule in the government's pipeline, from environmental limits to safety standards, is frozen at once, including rules that were nearly finished. Because the exceptions mainly cover military, personnel, and benefits administration rather than regulatory protections, the burden lands on the rules that constrain business conduct. A reasonable person could support reviewing costly rules individually; this bill instead halts the entire rulemaking apparatus, which is a much blunter instrument whose costs outweigh the savings for most households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary committees and then to two subcommittees in spring 2011, and neither panel ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Carter introduced the bill on March 29, 2011, and it was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee. [S1][S5]

In April 2011 it was referred to the Oversight Subcommittee on Regulatory Affairs, Stimulus Oversight and Government Spending, and in June 2011 to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law. [S5]
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013. [S1][S5]
Six Republican cosponsors joined the bill; no Democrat did. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections came out ahead, because the two-year freeze on new pollution, safety, and consumer rules never took effect. Regulated industries did not get the blanket compliance delay they would have gained from the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on federal protections

industries.industry: Regulated industries broadly (manufacturers, energy, chemical, and other firms facing federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have given every regulated business a two-year delay on complying with new federal requirements, saving compliance costs during the freeze. The public bears the corresponding cost of delayed health, safety, and environmental protections.

Agencies would have been barred from finalizing rules, stalling years of pending work, though the freeze leaves their existing rules untouched. Their interest in continuing to issue protections ran against the bill.

industries.industry: Businesses relying on benefit, grant, and contract rules
industries.note: The moratorium exempted rules on loans, grants, benefits, and contracts, so businesses and people depending on those programs would not have been affected by the freeze. [S2]
